Document: Nandigram, a small coastal town in West Bengal s East Midnapore district, was once the epicentre of a movement that redefined Bengal s politics. In 2007, the land agitation here did not just resist acquisition for a petro-chemical hub, it also dismantled a regime and scripted the rise of Mamata Banerjee. Nearly two decades later, the same ground and the same people tell a far more complicated story. In 2021, Nandigram delivered one of the most symbolic blows in Bengal s political history. It was almost an unthinkable political event. Bengal s chief minister Mamata Banerjee, who was seeking re-election for a third term, lost here to her former confidant Suvendu Adhikari. It was not just a defeat, it marked

the shift of a trusted lieutenant into her most formidable adversary. In 2026, the battle returned to Nandigram, yet again. However, the narrative has moved beyond personalities. While Banerjee avoided repeating her 2021 misstep, Adhikari opted to contest from two constituencies his home turf of Nandigram and Bhabanipur, considered Banerjee s stronghold. In response, Banerjee brought her close associate Pabitra Kar into the party fold and fielded him against Adhikari. Kar had been Subhendu s election manager for past elections and he is now his opponent. Malay Sinha, BJP s East Midnapore district president said, Kar does not stand a chance here. He was caught red handed while stealing from development funds and he was denied a ticket. That is

how he landed in the Trinamool party. Dada Suvendu has no threat from him." The question is no longer just who wins Nandigram, but what, if anything, has changed for the people who once stood at the centre of a revolution. The roads leading into Nandigram still carry the echoes of 2007. The Tehkali bridge, once a flashpoint of confrontation, now stands quiet, more as a reminder than a rallying point. The bridge witnessed Bengal s political churn. But beyond symbolism, the lived reality remains stark. Dependence on the government s cash dole has risen so did the migration. Villages still grapple with broken infrastructure, limited employment avenues, and a sense that the momentum of the movement never translated into

sustained development. For many residents, the land agitation brought visibility on the map, but not transformation. The promise was protection from displacement, but the expectation was progress. That expectation, many say, remains only partially fulfilled. I completed my ITI hoping it would lead to a stable job, but I m still unemployed. When I went to collect the financial assistance, I was turned away because they see me as a BJP supporter," said Kaushik Gatait, a young villager, his frustration reflecting a deeper sense of exclusion. Election cycles bring renewed attention roads get patched, outreach intensifies, leaders arrive. But once the ballots are cast, the urgency fades. Nandigram, it seems, has become a place politicians return to for legitimacy, not

necessarily for long-term investment. Every election, leaders come here and talk about the movement, about sacrifice and resistance. But after the votes are cast, nothing really changes for us," said Sunil Baidya, a local farmer. They all built their politics on Nandigram, whether it s Trinamool or BJP. But if you look around, where are the industries, where are the jobs? We stopped the land acquisition, but what came after that? No proper roads, no factories, no steady work. The movement gave them power, not us development," he added. The members of the resistance group Bhumi Uchhed Pratirodh Committee anti land eviction committee , are now in different political parties. The resistance group was formed in early 2007 in Nandigram

to oppose land acquisition for the proposed Special Economic Zone SEZ . Supported by the Trinamool Congress TMC , SUCI, and other forces, the BUPC blocked roads and prevented entry of CPIM party workers, leading to massive protests on the Tekhali bridge and the location became the flashpoint of the movement. Meghnad Pal, a senior member of the erstwhile resistance group said, People still believe in Subhendu Adhikari. At least, he did not desert them. Didi hardly came back to see how her compatriots are living. Instead, cases of political violence against us continued to pile on and now the number has crossed 500." Nandigram remains one of Bengal s most intensely contested constituencies, where every election feels like a

referendum. The rivalry between Mamata Banerjee and Suvendu Adhikari continues to dominate the narrative. For Suvendu, Nandigram is not just a constituency. It is the ground that validated his political break. For Mamata, it remains the site of a loss that still resonates. But beyond this high-voltage contest, the ground reality reflects a deeper churn. Political allegiance here is sharply defined, often cutting across villages and even families. Party flags are not just markers of support, they are lines of division. Locals speak of a constant state of mobilisation. Cadres remain active, tensions simmer beneath the surface, and the space for neutrality continues to shrink. Nandigram looks like a place wrapped in saffron flags and cut outs of PM Modi

and Suvendu. Despite repeated assurances of peaceful elections, apprehensions persist fuelled by past experiences and the intensity of the contest. In many ways, Nandigram today is trapped in its own legacy. The movement that once united people against a common cause has given way to a landscape of competing loyalties and enduring rivalries. Nandigram s story in 2026 is not just about a rematch between two political heavyweights. It is about a place that once changed Bengal, but is still waiting for that change to fully arrive.
